content: A hearing aid dispenser is an individual who is licensed to prescribe and distribute hearing aids. These professionals conduct hearing tests specifically to provide hearing aids to individuals experiencing hearing loss. They are trained in interpreting hearing assessment results, understanding hearing aid electronics, analyzing specifications, and performing modifications and programming of hearing aids. However, hearing aid dispensers are not qualified to diagnose hearing loss. All new trainees in the field of hearing aid dispensing are required to undergo a two-year training program under the supervision of a licensed hearing aid dispenser. Upon completion of this training, they are eligible to take the National Competency Examination to achieve Board Certification in Hearing Instrument Sciences. Advanced training is available through a two-year audioprostology program sponsored by the International Hearing Society. State licensure evaluations include both written and practical examinations to ensure competency. Every state in the United States licenses hearing aid dispensers to ensure public safety, with many states utilizing the standardized International Licensing Examination provided by the International Hearing Society. The minimum educational requirements for becoming a hearing aid dispenser vary by state. Hearing aid dispensers may work under audiologists, ear, nose, and throat (ENT) specialists, or in private practices. The average salary for a hearing aid dispenser can vary widely. As the population continues to age, there is a potential for a shortage of both hearing aid dispensers and dispensing audiologists. It is important to note that hearing aid dispensers should not be confused with audiologists. Audiologists are university-trained healthcare professionals who diagnose hearing loss through comprehensive diagnostic testing as part of auditory rehabilitation. Unfortunately, many audiologists have not received extensive training in the use of modern hearing instruments. Dispensing audiologists, however, have undergone additional training in hearing instruments, and many have also achieved National Board Certification in Hearing Instrument Sciences.
